name: Processing Difficulty Effect
description: Information that is harder to process can sometimes feel more effortful, serious, or valuable than easy-to-process information. But the effect is not one clean rule: difficulty can also backfire, confuse, or reduce trust depending on the task.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to dense expert copy, premium-service positioning, AI explanations, and cautionary friction: small increases in difficulty can sometimes signal effort or expertise, but too much disfluency can just create comprehension cost.
myth_risk_note: Thompson & Ince (2013) show disfluency signals competence in specific service contexts, consistent with the entry's existing partial status. But the broader claim that processing difficulty improves learning and reasoning is directly undermined by a failed multi-experiment replication (Eitel et al. 2014 replicated the effect in Experiment 1 but not in Experiments 2-4) and a meta-analysis finding null effects for disfluency in text-based learning (Xie, Zhou & Liu 2018) -- though that meta-analysis's own recall-performance and moderator results were themselves found methodologically shaky by a 2021 direct re-examination (its transfer-performance results held up). The effect appears narrowly robust in competence/effort judgments but not consistently supported across learning and reasoning tasks, and even the negative evidence there is contested rather than clean.
prevalence_note: Shows up in some behavioral-design, marketing, and writing-for-expertise discussions, but is far from a universally taught named UX law and is often implicit rather than explicit.

findings.description: Across four studies of service judgments, processing difficulty increased inferred agent effort and competence, which in turn raised expected service value. The effect weakened when subjective experience was made less relevant and could reverse for experienced rather than expected value.
findings.source_title: When Disfluency Signals Competence: The Effect of Processing Difficulty on Perceptions of Service Agents

findings.description: Reported to find an overall null effect of perceptual disfluency on text-based learning outcomes across the meta-analyzed studies -- disfluency did not reliably improve recall or transfer performance. However, a direct 2021 methodological re-examination of this exact meta-analysis (find-weissgerber-disfluency-reproducibility-critique) found the transfer-performance results held up as reasonably robust, while the recall-performance results and moderator analysis had real reproducibility problems raising doubts about their credibility. This description of the headline finding is drawn from secondary sources, not independently verified against the primary text this session.
findings.source_title: Null Effects of Perceptual Disfluency on Learning Outcomes in a Text-Based Educational Context: a Meta-analysis
